sections.h: 4 Maccabees: godly reason rules the passions
sections.b: 4 Maccabees is a speech built on one thesis: "godly reason is master in its own right over the passions" (4 Maccabees 1:1). It defines reason as the mind joined to a right way of life (1:15), sorts the passions under pleasure and pain (1:20-27), and pictures reason as a gardener who tames them (1:29). Its proofs come first from the law: the food laws (1:33-35), Joseph (2:2-3), the tenth commandment (2:5-6), the laws on loans, gleaning and enemies (2:8-14), Moses' anger (2:17) and Jacob's curse on Simeon and Levi (2:19). Then come the martyrs, beginning with the old priest Eleazar (5:1-6:30).

Against the Stoic ideal of a wise man free of passions, 4 Maccabees insists that no one can "cut out" craving, anger or malice; reason "is not the one who pulls up the passions by the roots. It is the one who wrestles against them" (4 Maccabees 3:2-5). God himself "planted the passions and habits all around" the human being, enthroned the mind over them and gave it the law (2:21-23). David's thirst is the proof: he felt the craving to the full and poured the water out to God (3:6-16).

common: 4 Maccabees teaches that reason trained by the law of Moses can rule every passion without destroying it.
uncommon: Some readers set 4 Maccabees 2:6 beside Romans 7:7-8 as two opposite readings of the same commandment: proof of reason's power, and the occasion of sin.

sections.h: 4 Maccabees: the four virtues as kinds of wisdom
sections.b: 4 Maccabees calls good sense, justice, courage and self-restraint "the kinds of wisdom" and makes good sense their ruler (4 Maccabees 1:18-19). Wisdom is the knowledge of things divine and human, and of their causes, a definition Cicero also gives as the old philosophers' (1:16), and it is "the training the law gives" (1:17). The Wisdom of Solomon names the same four (Wisdom of Solomon 8:7; see Hellenism). Eleazar tells the king that the law teaches self-restraint, courage, justice and godliness (5:23-24), and the speech says the mind that lives by the law reigns over "a self-restrained, just, good and courageous kingdom" (2:23).

sections.b: 4 Maccabees uses the Stoics' sorting of the passions (pleasure and pain, with craving and fear before them, 4 Maccabees 1:20-23) and some of their words, such as the mind as ruling "leader" (2:22). It parts from them on the main point: the Stoics taught that the virtuous person feels no passions, while 4 Maccabees says reason rules the passions but cannot root them out (1:6; 3:5). The king's argument that pork is nature's gift (5:7-9) and Eleazar's answer that the Creator made the law to fit nature (5:25-26) are a Jewish debate in Greek terms. Codex Sinaiticus and Venetus define reason with the phrase "right reason" (1:15).

sections.h: 4 Maccabees: the food laws as training and as test
sections.b: 4 Maccabees uses the food laws twice. First as training: when we crave sea creatures, birds and four-footed animals that the law forbids, "we keep away from them because reason has mastery" (4 Maccabees 1:33-35). Then as the test of loyalty: Antiochus forces every Jew to taste pork and food sacrificed to idols (4:26; 5:2). The king argues that nature gave the pig as food (5:7-9); Eleazar answers that the Creator allowed the foods that suit the soul and forbade those that work against it (5:25-26), and that a small sin weighs the same as a great one (5:19-21).

sections.b: For 4 Maccabees the law of Moses is the true philosophy (4 Maccabees 5:22). Wisdom is "the training the law gives" (1:17); God gave the law to the mind when he made human beings (2:23); and the laws on loans, gleaning, family, enemies and food all train reason to rule the passions (1:33-2:14). Eleazar says the law teaches self-restraint, courage, justice and godliness (5:23-24), and that breaking it in small things or great weighs the same (5:20). Paul, quoting the same tenth commandment, says the law gives knowledge of sin rather than power over it (Romans 7:7-8; Romans 3:20).

sections.b: Dying in the fire, the old priest Eleazar prays: "Be merciful to your nation. Let the penalty we pay on their account be enough for you. Make my blood their cleansing, and take my soul as a life in exchange for them" (4 Maccabees 6:28-29). He asks in so many words that a martyr's blood cleanse the nation (katharsion) and his soul stand as a life in place of theirs (antipsychon); the youngest brother's prayer in 2 Maccabees 7:37-38 comes close to it. It builds on Leviticus 17:11 and Isaiah 53, and the speech returns to it at 17:20-22. The likeness to Mark 10:45 ("a ransom in place of many") and Romans 3:25 is often noted; whether the New Testament writers knew this book is not shown, and Daniel Bailey warns against "paralleling Romans and 4 Maccabees prematurely".

common: Many scholars see in 4 Maccabees 6:28-29 and 17:20-22 the clearest Jewish witness before the church to the idea that a righteous person's death can atone for others.

sections.h: 4 Maccabees: Eleazar, the first martyr of the speech
sections.b: 4 Maccabees retells the death of Eleazar from 2 Maccabees 6:18-31 at length. Here he is a priest, an expert in the law and a philosopher (4 Maccabees 5:4, 35). He answers the king's arguments (5:16-38), is whipped, kicked and burned, and is likened to "a noble athlete taking blows" who defeats his torturers (6:10). He refuses even to pretend to eat pork, because he would become "a model of ungodliness for the young" (6:19), and he dies praying for the nation (6:27-29).

In 2 Maccabees Eleazar is "one of the foremost scribes" (2 Maccabees 6:18); 4 Maccabees calls him "a priest by birth, and in his understanding an expert in the law" (4 Maccabees 5:4). The speech gives him a debate with the king (5:5-38), a scene of torture (6:1-11), the offer to pretend (6:12-23) and a dying prayer for the nation (6:27-29). The first conclusion follows at once: "godly reason is master over the passions" (6:31).

4 Maccabees retells 2 Maccabees 3-6 in a few verses, with changes: Apollonius himself, not Heliodorus, comes for the temple money and is struck down by angels on horseback (4 Maccabees 4:1-14); Antiochus Epiphanes is wrongly called Seleucus's son (4:15); Jason pays 3,660 talents a year (4:17); and Antiochus, angered by joy at a rumor of his death, decrees death for anyone living by the ancestral law and tortures each Jew to make him taste defiling food (4:22-26). The speaker calls this "the proof from the history of self-restrained reason" (3:19).

4 Maccabees calls Onias "a fine and good man" who held the high priesthood for life (4 Maccabees 4:1). His rival Simon informs on the temple treasury, and when Apollonius falls half dead in the temple court, Onias prays for him, wary that the king might suspect a human plot (4:13), as in 2 Maccabees 3:31-33. Antiochus then removes Onias and sells the office to his brother Jason (4:16-17).

4 Maccabees names "King Seleucus Nicanor of Asia" as the one who paid for the temple service (4 Maccabees 3:20), where 2 Maccabees 3:3 has only "Seleucus"; the king meant is Seleucus IV, and "Nicanor" seems to confuse him with Seleucus I Nicator. It calls Antiochus IV his son (4:15), though he was his brother (Appian, Syrian Wars 45). Apollonius is governor "of Syria, Phoenicia and Cilicia" (4:2), a grouping that, in James Rochford's summary of David deSilva, was formed at some point between AD 19 and 72 and so may point to the book's date.

4 Maccabees retells 2 Samuel 23:13-17 as a lesson in self-control. After a day of battle, David craves the water in the enemy's hands; two young soldiers bring it from a spring in the enemy camp; and David, judging that the drink was "counted as worth the same as blood", sets reason against his craving and pours it out to God (4 Maccabees 3:6-16). In Samuel there are three warriors and a well at Bethlehem's gate.

"The self-restrained Joseph" is 4 Maccabees' first example: young and in his prime, he made the passions' sting powerless by reason (4 Maccabees 2:2-3). The speech reads his refusal of Potiphar's wife (Genesis 39:7-12) as a victory of reason over desire.

4 Maccabees calls Jacob "our all-wise father" and argues from his deathbed words on Simeon and Levi, "Their anger be cursed" (Genesis 49:7), that anger can be ruled by reason: he would not curse what could not be helped (4 Maccabees 2:19-20).

4 Maccabees quotes "You must not crave your neighbor's wife, or anything at all that belongs to your neighbor" and argues that, since the law forbids craving, reason must be able to rule it (4 Maccabees 2:5-6). Paul quotes the same commandment to show how the law made him know sin (Romans 7:7-8).

sections.h: Angels at the treasury in 4 Maccabees
sections.b: In 4 Maccabees Apollonius comes for private money stored in the temple treasuries. The priests, women and children pray, and angels on horseback appear from heaven with flashing weapons; Apollonius falls half dead "in the court of the temple that is open to all peoples" and begs the Hebrews to pray for him (4 Maccabees 4:7-12). The story is 2 Maccabees 3, told more briefly.

Eleazar expects that "the fathers will welcome me pure" (4 Maccabees 5:37), and the speech later says the martyrs are received by Abraham, Isaac and Jacob (13:17) and stand by the divine throne (17:18). 4 Maccabees speaks of the souls of the righteous living with God, where 2 Maccabees speaks of the raising of the body (2 Maccabees 7:9).

4 Maccabees says Jason made the nation give up its way of life and built a gymnasium on top of the citadel (4 Maccabees 4:19-20). Antiochus later argues like a Greek philosopher: the Jewish religion is not philosophy, nature gave the pig as food, and any god would forgive what is done under force (5:6-13). The book answers Greek culture in its own language: the law is the true philosophy (5:22-24).
